gbs333-b93434-d1e106.summary: Opens the single question of this distinction, restating the question-title: whether the power to sin was granted by God to the rational creature. Notes that the question depends on what was said above at distinction 37, where it was treated whether God is the cause of sin, and that the present discussion can therefore proceed more briefly.
claims: The question asks whether the power to sin was granted by God to the rational creature.
This question depends on distinction 37, which treated whether God is the cause of sin, so it can be treated more briefly here.

gbs333-b93434-d1e134.summary: First notandum: defines the power to sin as the power by which the will can will, not will, or refuse to will contrary to the law it is bound to obey. In reality this power is nothing other than free choice, or freedom of the will, by which the will can go either way in a contradictory pair; this freedom is not distinct from the will but is the will itself, since 'freedom' adds nothing to the will taken absolutely, but connotes only that the will, regarding an object shown to it by the intellect, can elicit or not elicit an act (will or not will) without any change occurring in the object or the will. This power therefore adds nothing to the will, whether absolute or relative, but simply expresses the nature of the will as created by God in this way (with fuller treatment at distinction 25).
claims: The power to sin is the power by which the will can will, not will, or refuse to will against the law it must obey.
This power is really nothing other than free choice / freedom of the will, by which the will can go either way in a contradictory pair.

Freedom is not distinct from the will but is identical with it; it adds nothing to the will, whether absolutely or relatively, but only connotes the will's capacity to elicit or not elicit an act toward an object without any change in object or will.
This power simply expresses how God created the nature of the will; fuller treatment is at distinction 25.

gbs333-b93434-d1e178.summary: Second notandum: freedom is always good, even though its abuse can be bad; the power (potentia) to do evil or sin is not itself evil, but good, and indeed the root of human honor and praise, as commended in Ecclesiasticus 31:10 ('who could have transgressed and did not'). Nothing is praiseworthy in doing good where there is no possibility of doing evil. The paragraph then quotes Jerome's letter to the virgin Demetrias at length: a man is not less truly good for being able to do evil, nor should nature's own inviolability be bound to a necessity of immutable good, since the honor and dignity of our rational nature consists precisely in this twofold freedom; there would be no virtue at all in persevering in the good if one could not have turned to evil; the best Creator willed that we be capable of both, commanding only the one (good) and granting the capacity for the other so that we might, from our own will, conform our will to his; hence even the fact that we can do evil is itself good, because it makes the good part better; and nothing sets the rational creature above the rest except that, while all other things possess good only by condition and necessity, the rational creature alone possesses it also by will.
claims: Freedom is always good; only its abuse (misuse) is bad, not the power/freedom itself.
The power to do evil or sin is not evil but good, and is the root of human honor and praise (Eccli. 31:10).
It is not praiseworthy to do good where one lacks the possibility of doing evil.

Following Jerome (ad Demetriadem): a man is not less truly good for being able to sin; the twofold freedom (for good and for evil) constitutes the honor and dignity of rational nature; there would be no virtue in persevering in good if one could not have chosen evil.

God willed that rational creatures be capable of both good and evil, commanding only the good, so that they might conform their will to his from their own will; thus even the capacity for evil is itself good, since it makes the good better.
The rational creature is set above other creatures precisely because it alone possesses the good by will, not merely by condition and necessity.
concepts: voluntary vs. necessary possession of the good

gbs333-b93434-d1e268.summary: Third notandum: although the ability to sin evidences freedom, it does not belong to freedom's essence (ratio). The first part is proved because nothing lacking freedom has the power to sin, since every actual sin is voluntary, and what lacks will (the only free faculty) lacks the power to sin. The second part is proved because God and the blessed possess freedom yet lack the power to sin, since it is contradictory for God to be able to sin, and the confirmed blessed likewise cannot sin. This confirms the saying of St. Anselm that the ability to sin is neither freedom nor part of freedom, since it does not belong to freedom's essence; freedom could exist without that power (though not conversely), so it is not an integral part of freedom's definition nor does it increase freedom (the will is no more free for having the power to sin than without it, as Ockham shows at I, dist. 10, q.2). It is, however, a subjective part, in the way 'rational' is not the essence of 'animal' nor a part of it, yet nothing rational fails to be animal (taking 'rational' as an essential difference). Turning to article 2, the first, responsive conclusion is then stated: the power to sin was conferred on the rational creature by God. This is clear from Lombard's text and the authorities he cites, and is proved by reason: every freedom is conferred on the creature by God, and every power to sin is a freedom, therefore [it is conferred by God] — the inference is evident and the minor is clear from the notanda; the major is proved because every nature is from God, and freedom is a nature.
claims: The power to sin evidences (arguit) freedom but does not belong to freedom's essence (ratio).
Proof 1: nothing lacking freedom (i.e., lacking will) has the power to sin, since actual sin is always voluntary.
Proof 2: God and the blessed possess freedom but lack the power to sin, since it is contradictory for God to sin, and the confirmed blessed cannot sin.

This confirms Anselm's dictum that the ability to sin is neither freedom nor part of freedom; freedom could exist without it (not conversely), so it neither belongs to freedom's essential definition nor increases freedom, per Ockham (I, dist. 10, q.2).
It is nonetheless a subjective part of freedom, analogous to how 'rational' is not the essence or a part of 'animal,' yet nothing rational fails to be animal.

Article 2, first conclusion: the power to sin was conferred on the rational creature by God, per Lombard's text and authorities, and proved syllogistically: every freedom is God-given, every power to sin is a freedom, every nature is from God and freedom is a nature.
concepts: posse peccare vs. essence of freedom
impeccability of God and the confirmed blessed

gbs333-b93434-d1e349.summary: Second conclusion: although the will (or act) to sin is culpable and evil, the power to sin is itself commendable and good. The first part is proved: every sin is culpable and evil; the will to sin is a sin; therefore [the will to sin is culpable and evil] — 'will' here is taken for the act of willing, not for the faculty (potentia), following Augustine's statement that nothing is as much in the will's power as the will itself, since the reason for sin is found primarily in the act of willing (the prior ground of freedom and voluntariness). The second part is proved by the authority of Jerome cited in the second notandum, and by reason: the nature of the will is commendable and good because it is constituted in an eminent species of creature; but the power to sin is the nature of the will, being its freedom, as shown in the first conclusion; therefore [the power to sin is good].
claims: Second conclusion: the will/act to sin is culpable and bad, but the power to sin is commendable and good.

Proof of the first part: every sin is culpable and bad; the will to sin is a sin; here 'will' denotes the act of willing (per Augustine, nothing is as much in the will's power as the will itself), not the faculty.

Proof of the second part: the will's nature is good because it belongs to an eminent species of creature; the power to sin is (per the first conclusion) identical with the will's nature (its freedom); therefore it is good.
concepts: culpability of the act vs. goodness of the faculty
Augustine on the will's power over itself
identity of potentia peccandi with libertas

gbs333-b93434-d1e404.summary: Third conclusion: the power to sin, though it exalts nature sublimely, is not perfectio simpliciter (an unqualified perfection). The first part is proved because it is precisely in this that all the honor of our nature consists, as Jerome says, and because the power to sin is the freedom of the will, which belongs only to the rational creature, which sublimely exceeds every irrational creature. The second part is proved because it is not better, in any given case, to have it than not to have it; therefore it is not perfectio simpliciter — the inference holding by the very definition (quid nominis) of 'perfection simpliciter' given by St. Anselm. The antecedent is clear because in God and the blessed it is better not to have it than to have it: whatever is not in God is better not had than had, otherwise God would lack some perfection and thus not be simply perfect.
claims: Third conclusion: the power to sin exalts nature sublimely but is not perfectio simpliciter.
Proof of the first part: it grounds all the honor of our nature (per Jerome) and is the freedom of the will proper to the rational creature, which exceeds all irrational creatures.

Proof of the second part: it is not better to have it than not (per Anselm's definition of perfectio simpliciter), since in God and the blessed it is better not to have it than to have it — for whatever is absent from God is better absent than present, or else God would lack a perfection and not be simply perfect.
concepts: impeccability as a mark of divine perfection

gbs333-b93434-d1e448.summary: Adds a further proof of the third conclusion's second part: whatever expresses a perfection simpliciter belongs to God; the power to sin does not belong to God; therefore it is not perfectio simpliciter — the inference following as at IV Sent. (dist. 44's material). The antecedent is proved because God cannot sin; indeed, God's being able to sin is contradictory, since it would imply his being able to act against his own will, which is itself a contradiction (willing and not willing the same thing at once), and to sin is precisely to act against the rule of the will — but God's own will is its own rule, being essentially right. Therefore, God's being able to sin amounts to his being able to act against his own will, i.e., to do and not do the same thing, which is contradictory. In the same way it is contradictory for the confirmed blessed to be able to sin while their confirmation stands, though it is not simply (absolutely) impossible that they sin, as was already established above concerning the confirmation of the angels at distinction 7.
claims: Further proof: whatever is a perfectio simpliciter belongs to God; the power to sin does not belong to God; therefore it is not perfectio simpliciter.

The antecedent is proved because God's being able to sin is contradictory: it would mean God could act against his own will, which is itself essentially right and its own rule, so this amounts to willing and not willing the same thing.

Analogously, it is contradictory for the confirmed blessed to sin while their confirmation stands, though not absolutely (simpliciter) impossible in itself, per the earlier discussion of angelic confirmation at distinction 7.
concepts: God's will as its own rule

gbs333-b93434-d1e505.summary: Opens article 3 with the first doubt raised against the first conclusion (that the power to sin is God-given), using arguments of St. Bonaventure: to be able to sin is to be able to fail (deficere); but the ability to fail is not a power (potentia) but an impotence, just as being able to die is [an impotence, not a power].
claims: Objection 1 (Bonaventure): to be able to sin is to be able to fail; but the ability to fail is not a power but an impotence, as with the ability to die; hence the power to sin should not be attributed to God as its source in the way a genuine potentia is.

gbs333-b93434-d1e518.summary: A second objection: the act of sinning is not from God; therefore neither is the power to sin. The inference holds because act and power come from the same source.
claims: Objection 2: since the act of sinning is not from God, and act and power come from the same source, the power to sin cannot be from God either.
concepts: act and potency from the same principle

gbs333-b93434-d1e530.summary: A third objection: glory heals nature; but glory removes the power to sin; therefore the power to sin is not from God, since glory does not remove from nature what is from God.
claims: Objection 3: glory is nature's remedy and removes the power to sin, yet glory does not remove from nature anything that is from God; therefore the power to sin is not from God.
concepts: glorification and the removal of peccability

gbs333-b93434-d1e541.summary: A fourth objection: the power to sin is a power of acting against God; therefore it is not from God, since God, being supremely in accord with himself, does nothing against himself, and so cannot be the source of a power to act against himself.
claims: Objection 4: the power to sin is a power of acting against God; God, being supremely self-consistent, acts in nothing against himself and so cannot be the source of a power directed against himself.
concepts: potentia peccandi as acting against God

gbs333-b93434-d1e554.summary: A fifth objection: everything in man has an exemplar in God to which it is assimilated; but through the power to sin man is not assimilated to God, but rather to the devil; therefore [the power to sin is not from God].
claims: Objection 5: everything in man has a divine exemplar to which it is assimilated; the power to sin assimilates man to the devil rather than to God; therefore the power to sin is not from God.
concepts: assimilation to God vs. to the devil

gbs333-b93434-d1e563.summary: Reports that St. Bonaventure raises these arguments but does not resolve them, using them instead to establish a distinction: the power to sin, considered as to its substrate, is from God, but considered as to the deformity that is formally present in sin, it is not from God — indeed, under that latter consideration, 'being able to sin' is not truly a power at all but a non-power. The author then gives his own resolution: since the power to sin is something absolute in man — namely freedom itself — which does not vary according to how we consider it (a thing does not become other, nor relate otherwise to what is considered of it, merely because of a different consideration on our part, unless the considerations themselves are imported into the predicate), it must simply be granted, without qualification, that the power to sin is from God, however it is considered. What is true is that the disordering (deordinatio), taken as a pure privation — since it is not any being (ens) at all — is not from God nor from any positive cause; but that privation is not the power to sin.
claims: Bonaventure uses the five preceding arguments not to deny that the power to sin is from God but to distinguish: as to its substrate it is from God; as to the deformity formally present in sin it is not, and under that aspect 'being able to sin' is really a non-power.

The author's own resolution: the power to sin is something absolute in man (freedom itself), invariant under differing considerations; hence it must simply be granted, without qualification, that the power to sin is from God, however considered.

The moral disorder (deordinatio) in sin, taken as pure privation (not any being), is not from God or from any positive cause — but this privation is distinct from, and not identical to, the power to sin itself.
concepts: invariance of a thing under differing considerations

gbs333-b93434-d1e661.summary: Addresses a further difficulty raised from the preceding solution: if to be able to fail (posse deficere, i.e. to sin) is not truly a power, then it might seem God is not omnipotent, since he does not have every 'posse.' The response is that God is not called omnipotent because he has every possible 'posse' whatsoever — he cannot, for instance, have the nature of a stone or a non-living nature — but because he can do (facere) everything doable (factibile), that is, everything positive other than himself; and in this sense he can indeed bring about everything positive that is present in sin.
claims: Objection: if posse deficere (the power to sin) is not truly a power, God, lacking it, would seem not omnipotent, since he would not have every 'posse.'

Reply: omnipotence does not mean having every conceivable 'posse' (God cannot, e.g., have the nature of a stone), but rather being able to do (facere) every doable (factibile) thing, i.e., every positive reality other than himself — including whatever positive element is present in sin.

gbs333-b93434-d1e683.summary: Replies to the second objection (art. 3) by denying its assumption: the act of sinning is indeed from God, yet God is not thereby a sinner, as was shown above at distinction 37.
claims: Reply to objection 2: the act of sinning is in fact from God, but this does not make God a sinner, per the earlier discussion at distinction 37.
concepts: God as cause of the act of sin without being a sinner

gbs333-b93434-d1e693.summary: Replies to the third objection by denying that glory removes from nature only what is not from God: glory removes corruptibility from nature, yet corruptibility naturally follows created nature simply because it is made from nothing; likewise glory removes from the blessed faith and hope, which are nonetheless gifts of God. Hence glory's removal of the power to sin does not show that power was not from God.
claims: Reply to objection 3: it is false that glory removes from nature only what is not from God — glory removes corruptibility, which naturally follows created nature (as made ex nihilo), and it also removes faith and hope, both of which are gifts of God.
Therefore glory's removal of the power to sin is no proof that this power was not God-given.
concepts: creation ex nihilo and natural corruptibility
faith and hope as gifts removed in glory

gbs333-b93434-d1e711.summary: Replies to the fourth objection by distinguishing the antecedent according to the sense of 'against God': either against God's will of good pleasure together with its consequent, in which case no creature has power to act against God (nor against his antecedent will, or the will signified by precept or counsel), so the antecedent would be false in that sense; or against God's preceptive will, in which sense the antecedent is true, since the power to sin is precisely the power of acting against the preceptive will — and the proof given in the objection concerns exactly this first sense (acting against God simpliciter), not the sense in which the antecedent is actually true.
claims: Reply to objection 4: 'against God' must be distinguished — against God's will of good pleasure (and its consequent) is impossible for any creature, so the antecedent is false in that sense; against God's preceptive will is possible, and it is in this sense that the antecedent (that the power to sin is a power against God) is true.
The objection's proof was directed at the first (false) sense of 'against God,' not the second (true) sense, and so does not establish its conclusion.

gbs333-b93434-d1e744.summary: Replies to the fifth objection: a created thing's exemplar in God is nothing other than divine cognition, which is not really simultaneous with any creature, being infinitely distant from each; yet it can be called a 'likeness' insofar as it is a distinct cognition of all things, just as a mental concept is called a likeness of the things it represents — and this is the only sense in which exemplars or ideas exist in God: an idea, insofar as it names an exemplar to which an agent acting through intellect looks in producing the thing exemplified (as shown at I, dist. 35), is not something real in God but an object known, as stated there. Man is, moreover, assimilated to God precisely through the power to sin, since that power is the will's freedom, and by this freedom he is assimilated to God, who is most free; the more a person conforms and submits his will to God's, the freer and more perfect he becomes, for according to Boethius the highest freedom is to be governed by, and to obey, justice. The paragraph, and the question, close with a doxological invocation asking that this freedom be granted by the God who is Alpha and Omega, beginning and end of all his creation, one and triune, blessed above all forever. Amen.
claims: Reply to objection 5: a creature's exemplar in God is simply divine cognition, which is called a 'likeness' only insofar as it is a distinct representation of the thing, analogous to how a mental concept represents what it knows; this is the only sense in which ideas/exemplars exist in God — not as something real in him, but as objects known (per I, dist. 35).
Man is in fact assimilated to God through the power to sin, since that power is the will's freedom, and freedom is precisely the respect in which man resembles the supremely free God.
The more one conforms and subjects one's will to God's, the freer and more perfect one becomes, since (per Boethius) the highest freedom is obedience to justice.
The question closes with a doxological prayer to God as Alpha and Omega, one and triune, for the grant of this freedom.
concepts: divine exemplarism as cognition (not real forms in God)
ideas as objects known, per I d.35
Boethius on true freedom as obedience to justice

gbs333-b93434-d1e809.summary: The colophon (explicit) closing the whole work: it announces the completion of the Collectorium of the most learned Gabriel Biel, licentiate of sacred theology, on the second book of the Sentences. It is a scribal/editorial notice rather than part of the doctrinal argument.

gbs333-b93434.summary: This quaestio unica, closing book II, asks whether the power to sin was granted by God to the rational creature, a question dependent on the earlier discussion (dist. 37) of whether God is the cause of sin. Three notanda first clarify terms: the power to sin is really identical with the will's freedom (liberum arbitrium), not a further addition to it; that freedom itself is always good even though its abuse is not, since it is the very root of human dignity (per Ecclesiasticus and, at length, Jerome's letter to Demetrias); and that, while the ability to sin evidences freedom (since only free, willing agents can sin, and God and the confirmed blessed have freedom without it), it does not belong to freedom's essence, per Anselm and Ockham. Article 2 then draws three conclusions: (1) the power to sin was conferred on the rational creature by God, since all freedom and all nature come from God; (2) although the will or act of sinning is culpable, the power to sin itself is commendable and good, since it is identical with the will's freedom; (3) the power to sin, though it sublimely exalts rational nature above irrational creatures, is not an unqualified perfection (perfectio simpliciter), since it is better, in God and the confirmed blessed, not to have it than to have it — indeed it is contradictory for God to sin, since this would mean acting against his own will, which is its own rule. Article 3 confronts five objections drawn from Bonaventure, arguing in various ways that the power to sin cannot be from God (as a mere impotence rather than a potentia; because the act of sin is not from God; because glory removes it; because it is a power against God; because it fails to assimilate man to God's exemplar). The author reports that Bonaventure himself left these unresolved, using them only to distinguish the power to sin's substrate (from God) from the deformity in sin (not from God). The author's own resolution insists that the power to sin, being an absolute reality (freedom itself) invariant under differing considerations, must simply and without qualification be granted as from God; only the privative disorder (deordinatio) of sin, not being any positive being, is not from God. Each objection is then answered in turn: failing is a positive power only when it is the privation of an act in an apt subject (as with dying), and God remains omnipotent by being able to do everything positive rather than every conceivable 'posse'; the act of sinning is indeed from God without making God a sinner (per dist. 37); glory removes other things not-from-God-in-themselves as well (corruptibility, and even faith and hope, which are nonetheless divine gifts), so its removal of the power to sin proves nothing; 'against God' must be distinguished into the (impossible) sense of opposing his will of good pleasure and the (actual) sense of opposing his preceptive will, in which latter sense alone the power to sin operates; and man's exemplar in God is simply divine cognition (not a real form), so that man is in fact assimilated to God through the power to sin precisely because that power is freedom, and God is supremely free — the greater a person's free conformity to God's will, the more perfect his freedom, per Boethius. The work closes with a doxology and the scribal explicit marking the end of Biel's Collectorium on Book II of the Sentences.
claims: The power to sin is really identical with the will's freedom, not an addition to it; freedom itself is always good, though its abuse is not, and constitutes the root of human dignity.
The power to sin evidences but does not belong to the essence of freedom, since God and the confirmed blessed possess freedom without the power to sin.

The power to sin was conferred by God on the rational creature, is itself commendable and good (though acts/wills to sin are culpable), and sublimely exalts rational nature — yet it is not an unqualified (simpliciter) perfection, since it is better for God and the confirmed blessed not to have it.

Against Bonaventure's objections, the power to sin, as an absolute reality identical with freedom, must simply and unconditionally be granted as being from God; only the privative moral disorder in sin, being no positive being, is not from God.
Man is genuinely assimilated to God through the power to sin, since it is the will's freedom, and the highest human freedom and perfection consist in freely conforming the will to God's.
concepts: divine omnipotence as facere omne factibile
Boethius on freedom as obedience to justice
